answer: DeepWalk (Perozzi, Al-Rfou, Skiena, 2014) is a representation-learning method: it samples truncated random walks over the graph, treats each walk as a "sentence" of node tokens, and feeds these into a skip-gram language model (word2vec-style) to learn a low-dimensional, continuous embedding for every node. Classification is then performed on these learned vectors with an ordinary discriminative classifier (e.g., one-vs-rest logistic regression), so the graph structure is compressed into features that are reused across tasks. Graph kernels, by contrast, define a similarity function between whole graphs (or between nodes) by comparing explicit substructures such as paths, graphlets, subtrees, or random-walk counts, building a kernel (Gram) matrix over the training set, and then plugging that matrix into a kernel machine such as an SVM. Kernel methods therefore operate on explicit, hand-designed substructure counts and scale poorly with data size because the kernel matrix is quadratic in the number of examples and the feature space is often sparse and high-dimensional. The advantage DeepWalk gains is that it learns dense, compact latent representations automatically from unlabeled graph structure, capturing high-order neighborhood similarity without manual substructure design; it is online-capable and scalable to large graphs (the paper reports strong performance on graphs such as BlogCatalog, Flickr, and YouTube with a small fraction of labeled nodes), and its embeddings can be used as generic features for any downstream classifier, including settings where labels are sparse and the graph is very large.
